name: ZX Spectrum
description: Sinclair Research's 8-bit home computer, launched in the UK in April 1982. Its low price and colour graphics made it the UK's best-selling computer of its era and the start of a large British games industry. Its colour-per-8×8-block limit caused the well-known "attribute clash".

specs.memory: 16 KB or 48 KB RAM (128 KB on later models)

curiosities: Its rubber keys each carried BASIC keywords, which were entered with a single keypress.
Its case was designed by Rick Dickinson and its hardware by Richard Altwasser.
Unofficial clones were built in large numbers in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe.
In the US it was sold in modified form as the Timex Sinclair 2068.
story: Clive Sinclair wanted a home computer most British families could afford. Richard Altwasser designed the ZX Spectrum around a Z80 and one custom chip, with rubber keys and colour, and it launched in April 1982 for £125.

Teenagers wrote games for it in their bedrooms and sold them on tape through shops and magazines. Ultimate Play the Game, Ocean, Dinamic and Codemasters grew on it, and it was hugely popular in Britain, Spain and across the Eastern bloc, where clones were built.
It sold about five million units and started much of Europe's game industry. Sinclair sold its computers to Amstrad in 1986.
